items.title: [exporterhelper] Sending queue can deadlock when blocked offers are canceled
items.body:
### Component(s)

`exporter/exporterhelper`, `exporter/exporterhelper/internal/queuebatch`

### Summary

Exporter sending queues can deadlock when `block_on_overflow: true` and blocked offers are canceled.

On v0.157.0, a persistent metrics queue stopped at 5,995,714 of 6,000,000 items. Queue and sent counters stopped while the health endpoint remained responsive.

The context-aware [`cond`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/4908404e59e544297b989a6961ee918b6f84b606/exporter/exporterhelper/internal/queue/cond.go#L14-L62) tracks waiters separately from a size-one notification channel. While canceled waiters wait to reacquire the mutex and decrement `waiting`, two closely spaced completion signals can fill the channel and block the second signal while it holds the queue mutex. Reads, offers, completions, and `Size` then stop.

The production path is [`persistentQueue.onDone`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/4908404e59e544297b989a6961ee918b6f84b606/exporter/exporterhelper/internal/queue/persistent_queue.go#L393-L425). [`multiDone.OnDone`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/4908404e59e544297b989a6961ee918b6f84b606/exporter/exporterhelper/internal/queuebatch/partition_batcher.go#L320-L325) can produce the closely spaced completions. [#15468](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/pull/15468#issuecomment-4786651716) includes v0.153.0 stack excerpts reporting one completion blocked in `cond.Signal` and the rest of the queue blocked on the same mutex.

The same code remains on `main` at [`0ffbf34b9da4bd1e499f4eb82ab6c6a8b4669081`](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/0ffbf34b9da4bd1e499f4eb82ab6c6a8b4669081/exporter/exporterhelper/internal/queue/cond.go#L14-L62).

### Deterministic reproduction

We ran the test below unchanged against v0.157.0 commit `4908404e59e544297b989a6961ee918b6f84b606`. It fails with `Signal blocked while holding the condition lock`.

The lock-attempt barrier proves both waiters selected cancellation before either notification is sent; the test does not rely on sleeps or queue startup order.

<details>
<summary>Runnable cond_test.go</summary>

```go
// Copyright The OpenTelemetry Authors
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0

package queue

import (
	"context"
	"sync"
	"sync/atomic"
	"testing"
	"time"
)

func TestCondSignalDoesNotBlockBehindCanceledWaiters(t *testing.T) {
	locker := &observedLocker{lockAttempts: make(chan struct{}, 2)}
	c := newCond(locker)

	ctx1, cancel1 := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	ctx2, cancel2 := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	waiter1 := startCondWaiter(locker, c, ctx1)
	waiter2 := startCondWaiter(locker, c, ctx2)

	locked := make(chan struct{})
	notify := make(chan struct{})
	notified := make(chan struct{})
	go func() {
		locker.Lock()
		close(locked)
		<-notify
		c.Signal()
		c.Signal()
		locker.Unlock()
		close(notified)
	}()

	<-locked
	locker.observe.Store(true)
	cancel1()
	cancel2()
	<-locker.lockAttempts
	<-locker.lockAttempts
	locker.observe.Store(false)
	close(notify)

	select {
	case <-notified:
	case <-time.After(time.Second):
		t.Fatal("Signal blocked while holding the condition lock")
	}

	for _, waiter := range []<-chan error{waiter1, waiter2} {
		select {
		case <-waiter:
		case <-time.After(time.Second):
			t.Fatal("condition waiter did not return")
		}
	}
}

type observedLocker struct {
	mu           sync.Mutex
	observe      atomic.Bool
	lockAttempts chan struct{}
}

func (l *observedLocker) Lock() {
	if l.observe.Load() {
		l.lockAttempts <- struct{}{}
	}
	l.mu.Lock()
}

func (l *observedLocker) Unlock() {
	l.mu.Unlock()
}

func startCondWaiter(l sync.Locker, c *cond, ctx context.Context) <-chan error {
	entered := make(chan struct{})
	done := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() {
		l.Lock()
		close(entered)
		done <- c.Wait(ctx)
		l.Unlock()
	}()

	<-entered
	l.Lock()
	l.Unlock()
	return done
}
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Incident configuration</summary>

```yaml
sending_queue:
  enabled: true
  storage: file_storage
  sizer: items
  queue_size: 6000000
  block_on_overflow: true
  num_consumers: 1
  batch:
    flush_timeout: 5s
    min_size: 10000
    max_size: 10000
    sizer: items
```

</details>

### Expected behavior

`Signal` must not block while its caller holds the condition mutex. Cancellation must not stop unrelated queue work.

### Workaround

Setting `block_on_overflow: false` avoids this wait path after restart, but a full queue returns an enqueue failure instead of blocking. Restarting can restore progress but does not prevent recurrence with the vulnerable setting.

### Related but distinct

This matches the `cond.Signal` stack excerpts in #15468 and is distinct from the startup-recovery deadlock in #12532, whose separate capacity check was removed by #13330.

items.title: missing data with persistent queues enabled during network outages
items.body: ### Component(s) extension/file_storage/storage ### What happened? **Describe the bug** Observed a consistency issue in gateway-collector when the otlphttp exporter queue uses file_storage for persistent queue storage. When **gateway-collector egress** is blocked with a network policy, **gateway-collector** experiences a network outage for approximately **3 days and 16 hours**. During recovery the data missing from the **first 4 hours** of the outage window. This has been reproduced multiple times with different window outages, and the missing data always appears at the beginning of the network connectivity issue. **Steps to reproduce** 1. Configure **gateway-collector** with persistent queue storage using `sending_queue.storage: file_storage/telemetry-retention`. 2. Apply a network policy that blocks **gateway-collector egress**. 3. Create a network outage 4. Restore connectivity. 5. Review the exported telemetry and compare the recovered data against the outage duration. **What did you expect to see?** All telemetry buffered during the outage should be retained and exported after connectivity is restored, including data from the start of the outage. **What did you see instead?** The **first 4 hours** of telemetry are consistently missing. The remaining telemetry for the rest of the outage period appears to be preserved. ### Collector version Contrib 0.127.0 ### Environment information ## Environment OS: (e.g., "Ubuntu 20.04") Compiler(if manually compiled): (e.g., "go 14.2") ### OpenTelemetry Collector configuration ```yaml otlphttp: endpoint: tls: insecure: false insecure_skip_verify: false sending_queue: block_on_overflow: true queue_size: 15000 storage: file_storage/telemetry-retention wait_for_result: true retry_on_failure: enabled: true initial_interval: 5s max_elapsed_time: 10m max_interval: 30s batch: send_batch_max_size: 1000 send_batch_size: 500 timeout: 10s extensions: file_storage/telemetry-retention: compaction: check_interval: 1m cleanup_on_start: true directory: on_rebound: true on_start: true create_directory: true directory: timeout: 10s service: extensions: - file_storage/telemetry-retention telemetry: logs: level: info pipelines: logs/pod: receivers: [otlp] processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, batch] exporters: [otlphttp] ``` ### Log output ```shell ``` ### Additional context Am I missing something or my setup is incorrect? ### Tip [React](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments/) with 👍 to help prioritize this issue. Please use comments to provide useful context, avoiding `+1` or `me too`, to help us triage it. Learn more [here](https://opentelemetry.io/community/end-user/issue-participation/).

items.title: Implement Adaptive Request Concurrency (ARC) for HTTP and gRPC Exporters
items.body:
### Component(s) exporter/exporterhelper --- ### Problem statement The OpenTelemetry Collector is already used successfully in large production environments. This issue is not claiming that the Collector cannot process high telemetry volume in general. The specific problem is narrower: **The exporter sending path has no feedback loop between downstream health and outbound request concurrency.** Today, exporters using `exporterhelper` can configure queues, retries, and a fixed number of queue consumers through settings such as: - `sending_queue.enabled` - `sending_queue.queue_size` - `sending_queue.num_consumers` - retry settings These controls are necessary, but they are static. Once `sending_queue.num_consumers` is configured, the Collector continues attempting sends at that fixed concurrency even if the downstream backend is slower, overloaded, returning HTTP `429` / `503`, returning gRPC `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` / `UNAVAILABLE`, or temporarily capacity-constrained during a rollout, autoscaling event, shard relocation, noisy-neighbor event, or incident. This forces operators to choose one static value that must work for both healthy and degraded backend conditions: - If `num_consumers` is too low, the Collector underuses healthy backend capacity and builds unnecessary queue latency. - If `num_consumers` is too high, the Collector can amplify downstream overload, increase retry pressure, grow queues, and eventually drop data when queues or retries are exhausted. The missing capability is not simply “more retries” or “a bigger queue.” The missing capability is a way to reduce outbound request concurrency when downstream signals indicate overload, and increase it again when the downstream recovers. --- ### Why the existing exporting mechanism is not enough The current exporterhelper mechanisms solve important but different problems. #### Sending queue The sending queue buffers data when an exporter cannot send immediately. It helps absorb short disruptions. However, the queue does not know what concurrency the downstream can safely handle. If the downstream starts slowing down or rejecting requests, the queue can continue feeding workers at the same static concurrency until it fills. A queue is a buffer, not a feedback controller. #### Retry policy Retry handles transient send failures. It is required for reliability. However, retry alone can make overload worse when the sender continues draining the queue at the same static concurrency while the backend is already returning retryable errors. Typical failure loop: ```text backend slows down -> exporter requests time out or receive 429/503/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED -> collector retries -> queue grows -> same fixed number of workers continues sending -> backend receives more pressure -> more retries -> eventual queue overflow or retry exhaustion ``` Retries decide whether to try again. They do not decide how many concurrent sends are safe right now. #### Static `num_consumers` `num_consumers` controls the amount of parallel send work, but it is fixed. There is no single correct static value because the safe concurrency limit changes over time based on backend capacity, request latency, payload size, number of Collector replicas, backend shard/node health, network conditions, retry behavior, and traffic volume. Operators end up tuning `num_consumers` for one condition and accepting bad behavior in another condition. --- ### Concrete operational scenarios this is intended to solve #### 1. Collector autoscaling multiplies downstream pressure In Kubernetes deployments, Collector tiers often scale horizontally when ingest volume, CPU, memory, or queue depth increases. With static `num_consumers`, downstream request concurrency grows linearly with the number of Collector replicas: ```text effective max outbound requests = collector replicas × num_consumers ``` Example: ```text 10 Collector replicas × 30 consumers = 300 possible concurrent sends 50 Collector replicas × 30 consumers = 1,500 possible concurrent sends ``` The per-pod configuration did not change, but downstream pressure increased 5x. This is especially risky during incidents because scale-out often happens when upstream volume is high or downstream capacity is already degraded. The Collector tier can unintentionally become an overload amplifier. Desired behavior: - each Collector instance observes latency and backpressure from the downstream, - in-flight sends are reduced when downstream health worsens, - concurrency gradually increases again when downstream recovers. #### 2. Downstream backend temporarily loses capacity Backends do not have constant ingest capacity. Elasticsearch, ClickHouse, Loki, vendor OTLP gateways, Splunk HEC, and intermediate Collector gateways may temporarily lose capacity due to shard relocation, node loss, rolling deploys, compaction / merge pressure, memory pressure, hot shards, hot tenants, storage saturation, throttling, autoscaling lag, or noisy-neighbor traffic. Example: ```text Healthy backend capacity supports ~100 concurrent export requests. During shard relocation or node loss, safe capacity drops to ~25 concurrent requests. Collector configuration remains num_consumers: 100. Collector continues sending up to 100 concurrent requests. Backend rejects or delays requests. Retries increase. Queue grows. Eventually data is dropped if the queue fills or retry time expires. ``` Desired behavior: - outbound concurrency shrinks when request duration increases or explicit backpressure appears, - the Collector continues making progress at a lower safe concurrency, - concurrency recovers gradually after the backend stabilizes. #### 3. Static tuning creates a safety-vs-throughput tradeoff Operators currently have to choose between: ```text low num_consumers = safer during incidents, but underutilizes healthy backend capacity high num_consumers = better throughput when healthy, but unsafe during downstream degradation ``` This is the core operational problem. The best value is not static. A value that is safe during backend degradation may be too conservative during normal operation. A value that gives good throughput during normal operation may overload the backend during degradation. Desired behavior: - allow higher effective throughput when the backend is healthy, - reduce in-flight concurrency when backend signals degrade, - avoid requiring operators to constantly retune one static value. #### 4. Tiered Collector deployments propagate overload Many production deployments use tiered Collectors: ```text applications / agents -> local or node Collectors -> regional gateway Collectors -> aggregation Collectors -> backend ``` If a downstream Collector tier or final backend starts refusing data, upstream Collectors may continue sending at fixed concurrency until retries and queues are exhausted. Current behavior: - downstream returns retryable errors or becomes slow, - upstream Collector keeps the same fixed send concurrency, - queues grow upstream, - retry pressure increases, - data may be dropped when queue or retry limits are exceeded. Desired behavior: - upstream Collector detects latency or backpressure from the next hop, - reduces in-flight sends, - avoids worsening the downstream incident, - keeps data moving at the highest safe rate. This is related to the class of problems where downstream Collectors refuse data under memory pressure and upstream Collectors need to respond more gracefully instead of continuing to send at a fixed concurrency. #### 5. Cross-region or variable-latency export paths Some Collector deployments export telemetry across regions, availability zones, or cloud boundaries. In these environments, request RTT can vary significantly even when the backend is not returning explicit errors. With static `num_consumers`, operators must choose a value that is safe during high-latency periods. That value may underuse available capacity during normal low-latency periods. Desired behavior: - use request duration as an early signal, - gradually reduce concurrency when RTT rises, - gradually increase concurrency when RTT returns to normal, - reduce queue growth without requiring constant manual retuning. --- ### Real-world precedent This problem is not unique to the OpenTelemetry Collector. Other telemetry and distributed systems have already addressed the same class of issue: a client can send faster than the downstream can safely process, and static limits are either too conservative during healthy periods or too aggressive during degraded periods. #### Vector Vector added Adaptive Request Concurrency for HTTP-based observability sinks because static outbound limits were not enough for destinations such as Elasticsearch and ClickHouse. Vector describes ARC as a feature that removes static rate limits and automatically optimizes HTTP concurrency based on downstream responses using a feedback loop inspired by TCP congestion control: - [Vector ARC documentation](https://vector.dev/docs/architecture/arc/) - [Vector ARC announcement](https://vector.dev/blog/adaptive-request-concurrency/) This is directly analogous to OpenTelemetry exporters: ```text Vector source/transform -> HTTP sink -> Elasticsearch/ClickHouse/etc. OTel receiver/processor -> exporterhelper queue -> exporter -> backend ``` The Collector has queues and retries, but it does not currently have Vector’s feedback loop that changes outbound request concurrency based on downstream latency and backpressure. Vector’s own QA issue for automatic concurrency also validates the behaviors that should be tested for OTel ARC: finding the optimal value, backing off during failure, backing off when response times gradually increase, and backing off when response times suddenly increase: - [Vector automatic concurrency QA issue](https://github.com/vectordotdev/vector/issues/3255) #### Netflix Netflix introduced adaptive concurrency limits to improve behavior under extreme load and avoid cascading service failures: - [Performance Under Load: Adaptive Concurrency Limits @ Netflix](https://netflixtechblog.medium.com/performance-under-load-3e6fa9a60581) - [Netflix concurrency-limits](https://github.com/Netflix/concurrency-limits) The key observation from Netflix’s work is that enforcing a concurrency limit is not the hard part; determining the correct limit in a dynamic distributed system is the hard part. That maps closely to Collector export paths: ```text Collector exporter = client Backend / downstream Collector = server ``` When the downstream is degraded, continuing to send at the same static concurrency can create the same retry-storm / cascading-failure pattern adaptive concurrency is designed to avoid. #### Splunk Splunk HEC provides concrete examples of downstream backpressure signals that clients are expected to handle, including: - `503 Server is busy` - `503 HEC is unhealthy, queues are full` - `429 Too Many Requests` - `429 HEC queue is at capacity and cannot process any more requests` References: - [Splunk HEC troubleshooting documentation](https://help.splunk.com/en/splunk-enterprise/get-started/get-data-in/10.2/get-data-with-http-event-collector/troubleshoot-http-event-collector) - [Splunk Connect for Kubernetes issue showing `Server is busy`](https://github.com/splunk/splunk-connect-for-kubernetes/issues/555) - [Splunk Lantern: persistent queue for metrics and traces](https://lantern.splunk.com/Observability_Use_Cases/Optimize_Performance/Enabling_persistent_queue_for_metrics_and_traces) Splunk’s guidance shows that persistent queues, retry configuration, and sending queues are important mitigations. ARC would complement those mitigations by reducing future in-flight requests when Splunk or another backend is already signaling overload. #### OpenTelemetry The OpenTelemetry Collector scaling documentation already calls out the same operational gap: if a backend is too slow, data piles up in the queue, and adding more workers is not always helpful because it can put more pressure on the suffering backend. - [OpenTelemetry Collector scaling documentation](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/scaling/) Today, the operator can observe that the queue is high and the backend is slow, but the Collector does not have a built-in mechanism to automatically respond by reducing outbound request concurrency and then increasing it again after recovery. --- ### Why Retry-After / server pushback is necessary but not sufficient Server-side pushback is still important. Adaptive concurrency should not replace `Retry-After`, retryable error handling, or correct mapping of HTTP/gRPC backpressure signals. However, server pushback is reactive. By the time a backend returns HTTP `429`, HTTP `503`, gRPC `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, or gRPC `UNAVAILABLE`, the backend has already accepted the connection/request and spent resources deciding it must reject it. A client-side adaptive concurrency loop can use both hard and soft signals: - Hard signals: `429`, `503`, `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, `UNAVAILABLE`, timeout. - Soft signals: rising request RTT before hard failures appear. The goal is not to ignore server pushback. The goal is to reduce future in-flight sends based on downstream health signals the Collector is already observing. ```text Retry-After / RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED = explicit rejection after overload is visible. Adaptive concurrency = reduce pressure when latency/backpressure indicates the backend is approaching overload. ``` Both should work together. --- ### What ARC is intended to do Adaptive Request Concurrency would control outbound request concurrency based on request outcome and request duration. At a high level: ```text before export request: acquire permit according to current dynamic concurrency limit execute export request: call the existing exporter send path after export request: record duration and final error increase concurrency when downstream is healthy decrease concurrency when latency rises or backpressure appears ``` Signals: - request RTT / duration, - success, - retryable backpressure errors, - timeout / unavailable conditions. Expected behavior: - increase concurrency gradually while requests are succeeding and latency is stable, - decrease concurrency quickly when latency rises or explicit backpressure appears, - remain bounded by configured min/max limits, - release blocked waiters during shutdown, - preserve existing retry and queue behavior. --- ### What this proposal is not This proposal is not claiming that: - the Collector cannot process high volume today, - retries are unnecessary, - server-side backpressure is unnecessary, - ARC should be enabled by default immediately, - ARC should replace queue sizing, - ARC should replace backend capacity planning, - ARC should solve global fairness across all Collector replicas, - ARC should be hardcoded into every exporter. The goal is more specific: **Provide a way for exporter sends to be governed by downstream feedback instead of only static local configuration.** --- ### Proposed validation plan To address maintainer concerns, I propose validating the feature before asking for broad acceptance. The validation should compare at least three configurations: 1. Static low `num_consumers` 2. Static high `num_consumers` 3. Adaptive request concurrency Metrics to compare: ```text - throughput: events/s or MB/s - export request RTT p50/p95/p99 - export error rate - retryable error rate - retry exhaustion count - dropped telemetry count - queue size p50/p95/max - memory RSS p50/p95/max - CPU p50/p95 - recovery time after downstream degradation - ARC current concurrency limit over time - ARC permits in use over time ``` #### Experiment A: controlled mock backend Use a backend that can simulate: - healthy low latency, - sudden latency spike, - HTTP 429 / gRPC RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED responses, - partial recovery, - jittery latency, - complete outage and recovery. Expected result: - static low concurrency is safest but underuses healthy capacity, - static high concurrency improves healthy throughput but creates more retry/queue pressure during degradation, - adaptive concurrency approaches high-concurrency throughput when healthy and reduces concurrency during degradation. #### Experiment B: two-Collector reproduction Topology: ```text load generator -> Collector A -> Collector B -> backend/mock ``` Induce pressure on Collector B by limiting memory, adding latency, or forcing retryable errors. Expected result: - static high concurrency overloads Collector B faster, - static low concurrency avoids some overload but wastes capacity when healthy, - adaptive concurrency reduces pressure when Collector B returns backpressure or slows down. #### Experiment C: real backend test Run against a real backend such as Elasticsearch, ClickHouse, Loki, Splunk HEC, or an OTLP gateway. Suggested test: ```text 1. Establish healthy baseline. 2. Introduce degradation: - reduce backend nodes, - trigger shard relocation, - add artificial latency, - throttle ingest endpoint, - or induce 429/503/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. 3. Compare static low, static high, and adaptive concurrency. 4. Report the metrics listed above. ``` --- ### Evidence to be added I will add benchmark and/or real-environment results in this format:
Test Static low num_consumers Static high num_consumers ARC prototype
Healthy throughputTBDTBDTBD
Degraded throughputTBDTBDTBD
Retryable error rateTBDTBDTBD
Retry exhaustion / dropped telemetryTBDTBDTBD
Queue p95/maxTBDTBDTBD
Memory p95/maxTBDTBDTBD
Export RTT p95/p99TBDTBDTBD
Recovery time after degradationTBDTBDTBD
Test configuration details: ```text Collector version/commit: Exporter: Backend: Payload type: Payload size: Input rate: Queue size: Retry config: Static low num_consumers: Static high num_consumers: ARC min/max: Test duration: Failure/degradation injected: ``` --- ### Relationship to the merged component-interface RFC There is already a merged Collector RFC for public component interfaces: - [Component Interface Guidelines](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/main/docs/rfcs/component-interfaces.md) I am not proposing a separate RFC for the mechanics of how a public component interface should be shaped. Any exporter request middleware interface should follow that merged guidance. Based on that RFC, this should be modeled as an open / optional interface: - extensions opt in by implementing the capability, - exporterhelper discovers the capability using type assertions, - the interface should use only public types, - the package should include the companion function type for the method, - test helpers should be provided in the appropriate test package, - future evolution should happen through companion interfaces rather than changing the existing open interface. The remaining question for this issue is: **Do maintainers agree that downstream-health-aware outbound request concurrency is a problem the Collector should support?** If yes, I will shape the implementation according to the merged component-interface RFC. --- ### Proposed implementation direction, after feature intent is accepted The initial version of this issue proposed putting ARC directly into `exporterhelper`. Based on maintainer feedback, I agree that the ARC algorithm itself should not be baked directly into exporterhelper first. The better direction is: 1. Treat this issue as the intent discussion for adaptive outbound request concurrency. 2. Keep the ARC algorithm in an extension or external implementation first. 3. Add only the minimal exporterhelper hook needed for an extension to wrap outbound exporter request execution. 4. Model that hook as an open/optional component interface following the merged component-interface RFC. 5. Introduce the hook behind an alpha feature gate. 6. Provide a draft ARC implementation at the same time so maintainers can verify the interface is actually used. 7. Use benchmark and real-world data to decide whether ARC should later be accepted more broadly. The first implementation would be an ARC extension that wraps outbound exporter sends: ```text acquire concurrency permit -> call next exporter sender -> record request duration and final error -> adjust concurrency limit ``` This keeps exporterhelper lean while still allowing experimentation with adaptive outbound request policies. --- ### Relationship to dynamic batching / sharding This should not conflict with dynamic batching or sharding proposals. Dynamic batching/sharding controls how work is grouped and consumed upstream of the final export request. ARC would act at the final outbound request boundary, where the Collector is about to send data to the next hop or backend. Conceptually: ```text receive -> process -> batch/queue/shard -> outbound request concurrency control -> exporter send ``` The two mechanisms solve different problems: - batching/sharding: how to organize and parallelize local work, - ARC: how many outbound requests the downstream can safely handle right now. --- ### Desired outcome from maintainers Before continuing implementation work, I would like to get maintainer agreement on the feature intent: 1. Is the lack of downstream-health-aware outbound request concurrency a problem the Collector should support? 2. Is an extension-based ARC implementation the right first step, instead of putting ARC directly into exporterhelper? 3. What benchmark or real-environment evidence would maintainers like to see before accepting the feature? 4. Assuming the feature intent is accepted, is an open/optional request middleware interface following the merged component-interface RFC the right shape for the exporterhelper hook? I understand the concern about adding new configuration or extension interfaces. I will avoid pushing the interface as a standalone abstraction until the problem statement and validation plan are accepted, and I will provide a draft ARC extension showing the interface is used.

items.title: Throttle exporting from persistence queue to reduce memory consumption
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
My team and I have encountered an issue where our collectors consume high memory usage when re-ingesting telemetry from a file storage queue after a disruption event with our backend. In these tests we have simulated an hour of connection failures to the backend to let our file storage queue grow. After an hour has passed, we restore the connection and see the spike in exported telemetry and memory usage.
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0713ba70-0a28-4d79-95c7-f290c889a1d6)
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2be946b7-6738-4012-bddb-ba50e213a06b)
Here is an example of the behavior we see from the persistence sending queue during the test period. Notice how the sending queue immediately drops to zero after reconnecting to the backend.
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d523a6ca-e55c-4141-95ea-2b57584cac35)
It seems like on reconnect with the backend, anything in the file storage queue gets consumed into a memory queue. We are hoping to control this memory spike so we can ensure memory won't pass a certain threshold when running on windows VMs


**Describe the solution you'd like**
Is there a feature we can add that will throttle how quickly the consumers pull from a file storage queue and send to the backend endpoint? Something that allows us to configure how many batches are pulled from the queue over a specified time frame?

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We have tried utilizing the memory limiter and GOMEMLIMIT environment variable but neither have been successfully. My guess is the garbage collector won’t reclaim the memory since the telemetry is still being actively sent. We have also tried reducing the number of consumers and the size of batches but we are sill seeing the spiking.

**Additional context**
Collector version: v0.99 contrib
Tested on Windows 2016 server

Here is the config we used for testing in case there are any config changes we could make to improve memory usage with the current version of the collector.

```yaml
extensions:
  health_check:
    endpoint: localhost:4313
  file_storage/backup:
    directory: {Directory of Collector on the machine}
    compaction:
      on_rebound: true
      directory: {Directory of Collector on the machine}
      rebound_needed_threshold_mib: 100
      rebound_trigger_threshold_mib: 10
      check_interval: 5s

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
      http:

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 1024
  batch:
    send_batch_size: 8192
    send_batch_max_size: 8192
    timeout: 10s

exporters:   
  otlp:
    endpoint: "http://{IP of backend server}:4317"
    retry_on_failure:
      max_elapsed_time: 0
    sending_queue:
      queue_size: 1000
      storage: file_storage/backup
      num_consumers: 10
    tls:
      insecure: true
    

service:
  extensions: [health_check, file_storage/backup]
  telemetry:
```

items.title: Improving resiliency through disk buffering capability
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Currently, collector buffers all data in memory, which can lead to data loss in case buffer gets overfilled (e.g. during temporary exporter connection issues) or due to a sudden crash. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**

There should be a possibility to enable disk buffering capability. For example, exporter could buffer the incoming data on disk (up to the defined limit) and clear the buffer as data gets sent out. In case of restart, recovery process could happen, which would send-out the buffered data.

Perhaps this capability could be a good fit to `queued_retry` [helper](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/blob/master/exporter/exporterhelper/queued_retry.go), since it already manages send queues?

**Additional context**
[Gitter discussion](https://gitter.im/open-telemetry/community?at=5fd326c53dd3b251a4fc4629)
